items.s: Equals the coupon rate and stays fixed for the whole life of the bond.
items.w: Nominal yield is locked in at issuance and equals the coupon, so it never changes.

items.s: Annual interest divided by par value.
items.w: The nominal yield uses par value, a constant, as its denominator, so it stays unchanged.

items.s: A bond paying $25 semiannually on $1,000 par is always described by this 5% figure.
items.w: Coupon dollars over par give the nominal yield regardless of the price the bond trades at.

items.s: Annual interest divided by the bond’s current market price.
items.w: Current yield uses the market price as its denominator, unlike the nominal yield which uses par.

items.s: Rises when the bond’s market price suddenly drops.
items.w: With annual interest fixed, a lower market price in the denominator raises the current yield.

items.s: On a premium bond, this is the lower of the two yields.
items.w: For a premium bond the current yield falls below the nominal yield because the price exceeds par.

items.s: Described as trading on a 9.5 basis or yielding 9.5%.
items.w: Those expressions are the book’s alternative ways of quoting a bond’s yield to maturity.

items.s: The most widely quoted yield, built on the years remaining until the bond matures.
items.w: YTM is the most widely quoted bond yield and uses the time remaining until maturity.

items.s: The only meaningful yield for a zero-coupon bond bought for a college fund.
items.w: A zero has no current interest, so yield to maturity is its only meaningful yield quote.

items.s: Replaces the years to maturity in the formula with the years to the first possible call date.
items.w: YTC is calculated like YTM but substitutes the years to the first call date for maturity.

items.s: Includes any call premium payable on the call date in the calculation.
items.w: Yield to call counts the call premium paid at the first call date, which YTM never includes.

items.s: On a discount bond, this is the highest of the yields.
items.w: For a discount bond the investor recovers the discount faster if called, so YTC exceeds YTM.

items.s: Benefits the issuer, so the bond generally pays a higher rate than a straight bond.
items.w: Callable bonds are riskier for investors and therefore pay more than comparable non-callable bonds.

items.s: The issuer is most likely to use it when interest rates are declining.
items.w: Issuers call high-coupon bonds to refund at lower rates, as a homeowner refinances a mortgage.

items.s: Federal government bonds do not carry this feature.
items.w: The book states bonds issued by the federal government are not callable by the issuer.

items.s: The investor may demand early repayment if the bond’s rating falls.
items.w: A put lets the investor sell the bond back to the issuer when a predetermined event occurs.

items.s: Benefits the investor, so the bond pays less interest than a similar straight bond.
items.w: Because puttable bonds favor investors, they pay less interest than comparable non-puttable bonds.

items.s: Attractive in rising-rate environments because the holder can reinvest the repaid principal at higher yields.
items.w: A put allows investors to demand repayment early and reinvest in higher-yielding bonds when rates rise.

items.s: Applied to a bond bought at 88, so the cost basis rises toward par.
items.w: A bond bought at a discount has its cost basis adjusted upward each year toward par.

items.s: An investor buys at $940 with six years left, and the basis is $950 after one year.
items.w: Straight-line accretion adds the $60 discount divided by six years, or $10, to the basis yearly.

items.s: Used for a bond purchased below par, increasing the basis until it equals $1,000 at maturity.
items.w: Accretion moves the basis of a discount bond upward so it equals par at maturity.

items.s: Applied to a bond bought at 108, so the cost basis falls toward par.
items.w: A bond bought at a premium has its cost basis adjusted downward each year toward par.

items.s: An investor buys at $1,100 with five years left, and the basis is $1,080 after one year.
items.w: Straight-line amortization subtracts the $100 premium divided by five years, or $20, from the basis yearly.

items.s: Used for a bond purchased above par, decreasing the basis until it equals $1,000 at maturity.
items.w: Amortization moves the basis of a premium bond downward so it equals par at maturity.

title: Interest rate risk vs Reinvestment risk

items.s: A 30-year zero-coupon bond carries more of this risk than a 5-year 7% coupon bond.
items.w: Longer maturity and lower or zero coupons make a bond’s price more sensitive to rate changes.

items.s: Duration is the measure of how sensitive a bond is to this risk.
items.w: Duration measures bond sensitivity to changing interest rates, and longer duration means greater price sensitivity.

items.s: Rates rise sharply and the market price of an outstanding fixed-rate bond falls.
items.w: The inverse price and rate relationship is interest rate risk, the risk bond prices fall as rates rise.

items.s: The Fed cuts rates, so the investor must reinvest the $80 received each year at a lower return.
items.w: The book’s example shows periodic interest being reinvested at lower rates as reinvestment rate risk.

items.s: A zero-coupon bond has none of this risk, since there is no interest to reinvest.
items.w: Zero-coupon bonds pay no coupons, so they have no reinvestment rate risk.

items.s: A bond is called after rates fall and no available investment offers a similar return.
items.w: Call risk leads to the risk that no investment can match the return of the called bond.
